Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 111, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Tafsir of Surah Tabbat (Surah al-Masad)

It is Meccan.

His Exalted saying: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he.﴾ The occasion of the revelation of this surah is what Abu Mu'awiya [al-Darir, Muhammad ibn Khazim] narrated from al-A'mash, the paternal uncle of Amr ibn Murra, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) ascended al-Safa one day and said: "Ya sabahah!" So the Quraysh gathered, and they said to him: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "Tell me, if I informed you that the enemy would attack you in the morning or in the evening, would you not believe me?" They said: "Yes."

He said: "Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment." Abu Lahab said: "May you perish! Is it for this that you gathered us?" So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he﴾ to the end of the surah.

He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: This hadith was related to us by Abu Muhammad al-Makki ibn 'Abd al-Razzaq, who said: my grandfather Abu al-Haytham related to us, who said: al-Firabri related to us, who said: Muhammad ibn Isma'il related to us, who said: Muhammad [ibn Salam] related to us, from [Abu] Mu'awiya... the hadith.

His saying: ﴿and perish he﴾. Muqatil and others said: he lost. Al-Tabab (perishing) in the language is destruction, and it is also loss.

Al-Farra' said: The first is a supplication, and the second is a report. The first is His saying ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾, and the second is His saying ﴿and perish he﴾, in the sense of a report, meaning: and he has indeed lost and perished. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "and he has indeed perished" (qad tabbat).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 111, verse 2:

And His saying: ﴿What his wealth availed him, nor what he earned﴾ means: his wealth and his offspring do not repel from him any part of the punishment of God. Thus His saying ﴿nor what he earned﴾ carries the meaning of "nor what he begot" according to this view.

Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: It is far-fetched for mā (what) to mean man (who) in the language.

So His saying ﴿nor what he earned﴾ means: nor what he earned from the one who came (with the message) and the like of him. As for Abu Lahab, he was the paternal uncle of the Prophet, and his name was Abd al-Uzza. It is said he was called Abu Lahab (Father of the Flame) because of the blazing brightness of his face.

God, exalted is He, mentioned him by his kunya (teknonym) either because he was known by it, or because his name was Abd al-Uzza and He disliked to attribute his servitude (ʿabd) to anyone other than Him.

In the tafsir of al-Naqqash: Abu Lahab disowned the Banu Hashim and affiliated himself with Abu Umayya, and he said: "I shall not be from a people among whom there is a liar like Muhammad."

Among what is known from Tariq al-Muharibi is that he said: "I was in the market of Dhu al-Majaz, when suddenly I saw a young man saying: 'O people, say: There is no god but God, and you will prosper,' and behind him a man was pelting him with stones, and his heels were bleeding, and he was saying: 'O people, do not believe him, for he is a liar.'

He said: So I asked about them, and it was said: The young man is Muhammad, and the man behind him is his paternal uncle Abu Lahab."

.

And it is said regarding His saying ﴿What his wealth availed him﴾: that is, what thing did his wealth avail him ﴿nor what he earned﴾ when he entered the Fire?

He said: "He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame" (Q 111:3). It is said: "saliya al-shay'" means he endured its intensity and heat.

It is also said: "sallaytuhu" means I roasted it, and from this comes "shāh muṣallāh," meaning a roasted sheep. The meaning is: he will soon enter (yuṣlā) a fire, namely one of blazing flame, meaning one of flaring and kindling.

And His words: "and his wife" (Q 111:4), meaning: his wife will also burn (tuṣlā).

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 111, verse 4:

And His saying: ﴿the carrier of firewood﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: what al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that she used to carry thorns and throw them on the path of the Prophet (ﷺ) so as to wound his foot.

'Atiyya said: She used to throw thornbushes (al-'idah) on the path of the Prophet (ﷺ), and they were like a heap of sand before the Prophet's feet.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿the carrier of firewood﴾ means: the one who walks about with tale-bearing (al-namimah).

The poet said:

(Indeed the sons of al-Ajram are carriers of firewood... they are the slanderers in contentment and in anger.)

(Upon them be curse upon curse, and war.)

Her husband was Umm Jamil bint Harb ibn Umayya, the sister of Abu Sufyan.

It has been read as "ḥammālata al-ḥaṭab" in the accusative (naṣb) and in the nominative (raf'), the nominative meaning "she is the carrier of firewood," and the accusative meaning "I mean, the carrier of firewood."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 111, verse 5:

And His saying: ﴿Around her neck a rope of palm fiber﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions. The more apparent of them is that it is the chain which Allah the Exalted mentioned in His Book: ﴿In a chain, its length seventy cubits﴾. Al-masad is twisting and tightening, and he said: "Because it is tighter than iron." The second opinion is that the meaning of the verse is that she used to carry firewood with a rope of masad around her neck, and Allah the Exalted mentioned this for one of two reasons: either to show her baseness and contemptibility, or because she had reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with poverty, so Allah the Exalted afflicted her with something that is the work of the poor. It was also said: "A rope of masad" means a rope of hair whose twisting is tightened, and it was said: of palm fiber whose twisting is tightened.

It is related that when this surah was revealed, the wife of Abu Lahab heard it, took a stone (fahr) in her hand, and came seeking the Prophet, saying:

(We have dispraised Mudhammam, our father... and his religion we have defied... and his command we have disobeyed...)

By "Mudhammam" she meant Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Quraysh disbelievers used to revile him as "Mudhammam." When she came, Abu Bakr said to the Prophet: "This woman has come." He said: "She will not see me." So she entered and did not see the Messenger of Allah, and she said to Abu Bakr: "Where is your companion?" He said: "What is the matter with you?" She said: "It has reached me that he has satirized me, so I came to break his head with this stone." Abu Bakr said: "He has not satirized you." So she returned, stumbled over her cloak, and said: "Wretched is Mudhammam," and she departed.
